cards.title: 1.1 Historical Development of the Periodic Table (1/3)
body: **The Periodic Table of Elements is a systematic tabular arrangement of chemical elements organized by increasing atomic number, which highlights the recurring (periodic) chemical and physical properties of the elements.**

Classifying elements is crucial in chemistry. In the early 1800s, only about thirty elements were known, each with seemingly distinct properties. As new elements were discovered, scientists gathered more information, making it difficult to organize this knowledge. This led chemists to seek patterns, eventually giving rise to the modern Periodic Table, which provides a fundamental framework for understanding chemical behaviors.

Early classification attempts began by grouping elements simply into metals and nonmetals. In 1829, German chemist Johann Wolfgang Döbereiner attempted to organize elements into groups of three, known as **Döbereiner's Triads**. He noticed that when three elements with similar properties were written in order of increasing atomic mass, the atomic mass of the middle element was roughly the average of the other two. For example, in the triad of Lithium ($$6.9\text{ u}$$), Sodium ($$23.0\text{ u}$$), and Potassium ($$39.0\text{ u}$$), the average of Lithium and Potassium is $$\frac{6.9 + 39.0}{2} \approx 23.0\text{ u}$$, which matches Sodium. However, this triad system could not be applied to all elements and was of limited use.

In 1864, English chemist John Newlands arranged elements in order of increasing relative atomic mass and formulated the **Law of Octaves**. He observed that every eighth element exhibited similar physical and chemical properties, similar to the octaves found in music. While innovative, Newlands' system failed for elements beyond Calcium, as the pattern of eighth-element similarity did not hold for heavier elements.

cards.title: 1.1 Historical Development of the Periodic Table (2/3)
body: The major breakthrough in element classification belongs to Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869. Mendeleev organized the sixty-three known elements based on their atomic masses and chemical similarities, particularly their formulas when reacting with oxygen and hydrogen. He formulated **Mendeleev's Periodic Law**, which stated that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic masses. Mendeleev left empty gaps in his table for elements not yet discovered (such as *eka-Aluminium*), boldly predicting their physical and chemical properties. When Gallium was discovered later, its properties matched Mendeleev's predictions with remarkable accuracy.

Despite its success, Mendeleev's table had key limitations. It did not clearly place Hydrogen, could not accommodate isotopes (which have identical chemical properties but different masses), and contained mass-order discrepancies, such as placing Tellurium ($$127.6\text{ u}$$) before Iodine ($$126.9\text{ u}$$) to match their chemical families. These discrepancies were resolved in 1913 when English physicist Henry Moseley used X-ray spectra to prove that the **atomic number** (the number of protons in a nucleus) is the fundamental property of an element. This modified Mendeleev's law into the **Modern Periodic Law**: **The properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.**

cards.title: Newlands — Law of Octaves
body: By the 1860s more elements were known, and chemists looked for repeating patterns. In 1864–1865 the English chemist John Newlands arranged known elements in order of increasing atomic mass.
Newlands noticed that every eighth element seemed to show properties similar to the first, like notes repeating every octave in music. He called this the Law of Octaves.
Example idea: if you list Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, then Na (the 8th after Li in his listing) resembles lithium; K resembles sodium, and so on for the lighter elements.

Limitations: the law worked reasonably only for the lighter elements. It broke down for heavier elements; Newlands sometimes forced dissimilar elements into the same group to keep the octave pattern. New elements being discovered did not fit neatly. Many chemists rejected the musical analogy at first.
Despite its limits, Newlands helped establish that properties of elements repeat periodically when elements are ordered by mass — an important step toward the modern periodic table.

cards.title: Mendeleev’s periodic table
body: In 1869 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev arranged elements mainly in order of increasing atomic mass, but he also grouped elements with similar chemical properties into vertical columns (groups).

When the mass order conflicted with chemical similarity, Mendeleev sometimes adjusted positions. Crucially, he left gaps for elements that had not yet been discovered, and he predicted their properties (for example eka-silicon, later germanium; eka-aluminium, later gallium).
When gallium and germanium were discovered, their properties closely matched Mendeleev’s predictions. That success convinced many scientists that the periodic law was real.

Limitations of Mendeleev’s table: a few pairs of elements appeared in the wrong order if sorted strictly by atomic mass (e.g. tellurium and iodine; argon and potassium) because the true ordering principle had not yet been found. He also did not know about noble gases at first, and isotopes were unknown.

Contrast with Moseley: in 1913 Henry Moseley used X-ray spectra to show that nuclear charge (atomic number $$Z$$) increases by one from element to element. The modern periodic law orders elements by atomic number, which fixes the misplaced pairs and matches electron structure.

Summary: Newlands saw a repeating “every 8th” pattern; Mendeleev built a practical table with gaps and predictions based on atomic mass and properties; Moseley replaced mass with atomic number as the fundamental order.

cards.title: Historical development — from triads to atomic number
body: Döbereiner’s triads (1829): groups of three similar elements where the middle atomic mass was roughly the average of the other two (e.g. Li, Na, K; Cl, Br, I). This was an early hint of regularity, but only a few triads worked.
Newlands’ octaves: ordered by atomic mass; similarity every eighth element; failed for heavier elements.
Mendeleev: ordered by atomic mass with chemical groups, left gaps, predicted undiscovered elements; most successful 19th-century table.
Modern table (after Moseley): ordered by atomic number; periods and groups reflect electron configuration. Atomic mass still appears on the table, but atomic number decides position.

cards.title: 1.3 Electron Configuration and the Periodic Table (1/3)
body: **Electron configuration is the detailed distribution of an atom's electrons among various atomic orbitals and subshells in accordance with established energetic principles like the Aufbau principle.**

To understand why elements show periodic patterns, we must examine their electron configurations. In grade nine, we learned that electrons reside in main energy levels or shells ($$n = 1, 2, 3...$$ or K, L, M, N). In grade ten, we dive deeper: each main energy shell consists of one or more **subshells** designated by the letters **$$s, p, d, f$$**. The number of subshells in a shell is equal to its principal quantum number ($$n$$). For example, the first shell ($$n=1$$) has only one subshell ($$1s$$), while the second shell ($$n=2$$) has two subshells ($$2s$$ and $$2p$$).

Each subshell has a maximum capacity of electrons: an $$s$$ subshell can hold up to 2 electrons, a $$p$$ subshell can hold up to 6, a $$d$$ subshell up to 10, and an $$f$$ subshell up to 14. The total electron capacity of a main shell is determined by the formula **$$2n^2$$**.

cards.title: 1.3 Electron Configuration and the Periodic Table (2/3)
body: Electrons fill subshells in order of increasing energy. This filling order, known as the **Aufbau Principle**, is illustrated by a diagonal rule: $$1s \rightarrow 2s \rightarrow 2p \rightarrow 3s \rightarrow 3p \rightarrow 4s \rightarrow 3d \rightarrow 4p \rightarrow 5s...$$ Note that the $$4s$$ subshell is filled before the $$3d$$ subshell because $$4s$$ represents a slightly lower energy state than $$3d$$. For example, the configuration of Iron ($$Z = 26$$) is written as: $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^2 3d^6$$.

To simplify writing configurations for heavier elements, we can use the **abbreviated electron configuration** (noble gas notation). This uses the symbol of the preceding noble gas in brackets to represent the core electrons. For instance, Sodium ($$Z = 11$$), which has the full configuration $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^1$$, can be abbreviated as **$$[\text{Ne}]3s^1$$**, where $$[\text{Ne}]$$ represents the core configuration of Neon ($$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$$).

Based on their outermost subshell configurations, elements are classified into three major blocks on the Periodic Table: • **Representative Elements (s-block and p-block):** These elements belong to Groups IA through VIIIA. Their outermost electrons are filling $$s$$ or $$p$$ subshells. For example, Lithium ($$1s^2 2s^1$$) is an s-block representative element, while Carbon ($$1s^2 2s^2 2p^2$$) is a p-block representative element. • **Transition Elements (d-block):** Located in the center of the Periodic Table (Groups IB through VIIIB). Their outermost occupied configurations are filling the $$d$$ subshell of the $$(n-1)$$ shell.

For example, Iron ($$[\text{Ar}]4s^2 3d^6$$) is a d-block transition element. • **Inner Transition Elements (f-block):** Shown in two rows below the main body of the table. Their electrons fill the $$f$$ subshell of the $$(n-2)$$ shell. These consist of the **Lanthanide** (filling $$4f$$) and **Actinide** (filling $$5f$$) series.

cards.title: 1.3 Electron Configuration and the Periodic Table (3/3)
body: > **💡 Did You Know?**: The subshell letters $$s, p, d, f$$ do not stand for shapes. They were originally named by early spectroscopists to describe spectral lines: **s**harp, **p**rincipal, **d**iffuse, and **f**undamental!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: To easily write noble gas configurations, find the noble gas in the row directly *above* the element you are working on, place its symbol in brackets, and then continue filling subshells for the element's own row.

cards.title: 1.4 Periodic Regularities and Characteristics of Elements
body: **Periodic trends are the predictable, systematic variations in the physical and chemical properties of elements across periods and down groups of the Periodic Table.**

The arrangement of elements by atomic number reveals clear, repeating patterns in their physical and chemical behaviors. These regularities are governed by the balance between the nuclear charge attracting the electrons and the shielding effect of the core electrons.

cards.title: 1.4 Periodic Regularities and Characteristics of Elements — Core Periodic Trends (1/2)
body: • **Atomic Radius:** The distance from the center of the nucleus to the outermost occupied electron shell. • *Down a Group:* Atomic radius **increases**. Although nuclear charge increases, new energy shells are added, which increases the physical distance and shielding of outer electrons, overcoming the nuclear pull. • *Across a Period:* Atomic radius **decreases**. The number of shells remains constant, but the atomic number (nuclear charge) increases.

This increased positive charge pulls the outer electrons closer, reducing the size. • **Ionic Radius:** Cations (positive ions) are always **smaller** than their parent atoms because losing valence electrons reduces electron-electron repulsion, allowing the nucleus to pull remaining electrons tighter. Anions (negative ions) are always **larger** than their parent atoms because gaining electrons increases electron-electron repulsion, expanding the electron cloud. • **Ionization Energy (IE):** The minimum energy required to remove the outermost electron from a neutral gaseous atom. • *Down a Group:* IE **decreases**.

Outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and heavily shielded by core electrons, making them easier to remove. • *Across a Period:* IE **increases**. As atomic size decreases and nuclear charge increases, the nucleus holds outer electrons more tightly, requiring more energy to remove them. • **Electronegativity (EN):** A measure of an atom's ability to attract shared electrons in a chemical bond. • *Down a Group:* EN **decreases**. The shared electrons are farther from the attractive pull of the positive nucleus. • *Across a Period:* EN **increases** (excluding noble gases).

The smaller atomic size and higher nuclear charge allow the nucleus to exert a stronger pull on shared electrons. • **Metallic and Nonmetallic Characteristics:** Metals tend to lose electrons (low IE, low EN), while nonmetals tend to gain electrons (high IE, high EN). Metallic character **increases down a group** and **decreases across a period**, while nonmetallic character follows the opposite trend.

cards.title: 1.4 Periodic Regularities and Characteristics of Elements — Core Periodic Trends (2/2)
body: These properties also affect the chemical formulas of compounds formed across periods. For example, chlorides of period 3 elements show a distinct pattern based on valency. Group IA Sodium forms $$NaCl$$, Group IIA Magnesium forms $$MgCl_2$$, and Group IIIA Aluminium forms $$AlCl_3$$. As we transition to covalent nonmetals, Group IVA Silicon forms $$SiCl_4$$, and Group VA Phosphorus forms $$PCl_3$$. This periodic change in formulas directly reflects the valence electron configurations of the elements.

> **💡 Did You Know?**: Fluorine ($$F$$) is the most electronegative element on the Pauling scale with a value of $$4.0$$, while Francium ($$Fr$$) and Cesium ($$Cs$$) are the least electronegative at $$0.7$$!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: Remember the acronym **AIE**: **A**tomic radius trends are opposite to those of **I**onization energy and **E**lectronegativity. If atomic size increases, both IE and EN will decrease.

cards.title: 2.1 Forces of Attractions
body: **Chemical bonds** are the forces of attraction that hold atoms together: can be described as attractive forces.
Intramolecular bonds refer to the forces of attraction that hold atoms together within a molecule.
Generally, intramolecular forces are considerably stronger than intermolecular forces.

cards.title: Step by step: Forces of attraction
body: **Step 1:** Intramolecular forces (chemical bonds) hold atoms together inside a substance: ionic (transfer of electrons, metal + non-metal), covalent (sharing of electron pairs, non-metals) and metallic (cations in a sea of delocalized electrons).
**Step 2:** Intermolecular forces act between separate molecules and are much weaker than bonds.
**Step 3:** London (dispersion) forces exist between all molecules and grow with molecular size.
**Step 4:** Dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules (e.g. HCl); hydrogen bonds are especially strong dipole forces when H is bonded to N, O or F (e.g. H₂O, NH₃, HF).
**Step 5:** Stronger intermolecular forces → higher melting and boiling points.
**Example:** Water (M = 18) boils at 100 °C while hydrogen sulphide H₂S (M = 34) boils at −60 °C: water molecules are held by hydrogen bonds, H₂S molecules only by weaker dipole and London forces.

**Step 1: Calculate electronegativity differences ($$\Delta\text{EN}$$) for the options**
*   For $$\text{H}_2$$: $$\Delta\text{EN} = 2.1 - 2.1 = 0.0$$ (Nonpolar covalent)

steps.text:
**Step 1.** Sharing electron pairs forms covalent bonds:
- **Single bond:** 1 pair shared (e.g., $$ H_2, Cl_2, F_2 $$).

cards.title: How to classify an unknown solid
body: Ask four school tests: melting point high or low? Does the solid conduct? Does the melt/solution conduct? Does it dissolve in water? High melt + conducts only when molten/dissolved → ionic. High melt + never conducts + insoluble → giant covalent. Low melt + never conducts → simple molecular. Conducts as a solid and bends → metal.

Dot-and-cross: metals lose until they look noble; non-metals gain or share until they look noble. MgCl₂ needs two Cl because Mg gives two electrons. Covalent pairs sit between symbols; leftover dots are lone pairs. Lone pairs push — that is why water is bent and ammonia is pyramidal (named properly in Grade 12).

Hydrogen bonding is a special strong intermolecular force, not a fourth primary bond. It explains water’s high boiling point, ice floating, and DNA later. When water boils you break H-bonds between molecules, not the O–H covalent bonds inside a molecule — if you broke those you would make hydrogen and oxygen gases.

**Step 1: Compare relative strengths of intermolecular forces**
*   London dispersion forces (caused by temporary fluctuations in electron clouds) are the weakest.
*   Dipole-dipole forces (between permanent polar molecules) are of intermediate strength.
*   Hydrogen bonding (a exceptionally strong, unique dipole-dipole attraction involving FON) is the strongest of these three.

The correct increasing order is **London dispersion < dipole-dipole < Hydrogen bonding**.

body: **Step 1:** Molarity (M) = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution in litres (mol/L).
**Step 2:** Moles = mass ÷ molar mass, so mass needed = M × V(L) × molar mass.
**Step 3:** Mass percent = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100 %; mass of solution = solute + solvent.
**Step 4:** Dilution: the moles of solute stay the same, so M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
**Step 5:** Always convert mL to L (÷ 1000) before using molarity.

body: **Step 1:** pH measures acidity: pH = −log[H⁺]. The scale runs from 0 to 14 at 25 °C.
**Step 2:** pH < 7 acidic, pH = 7 neutral (pure water), pH > 7 basic (alkaline).
**Step 3:** Each unit of pH is a factor of 10 in [H⁺]: pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What happens thermodynamically when any chemical bond is broken inside a molecule?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Define bond breaking energetics**
To break a chemical bond, attractive electrostatic forces between atoms must be physically overcome.

**Step 2: Identify energy direction**
Overcoming these forces requires an input of energy from the surroundings. Thus, bond breaking is always **endothermic** (absorbs energy).

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The correct choice is **Energy must be absorbed (endothermic).**

options.C: Reactants are at a higher energy level than products.
options.D: The enthalpy change ($$\Delta H$$) is positive.

cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze exothermic thermodynamics**
In an exothermic reaction, heat is released because the reactants possess more total chemical potential energy than the products ($$H_{\text{reactants}} > H_{\text{products}}$$).

**Step 2: Relate to the energy diagram**
Therefore, on the vertical y-axis (Enthalpy/Energy), the reactants are positioned **higher** than the products.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
The correct statement is **Reactants are at a higher energy level than products.**
